integrity.anchor_registry_note: The corpus provenance gate verifies each anchor against the file that anchor names and stores no registry-level digest of its own. This digest is recorded so a signature also pins which anchor set was in force.
integrity.verbatim_block_note: The block in section 3 is the file's decoded text with any single trailing newline removed, which is what the markdown fences require. `record_sha256` above is over the raw file bytes and is the digest a signature refers to; this one is over the text as embedded, so a verifier can compare either.

value: These are the interpretations this corpus made. They are not the interpretations the standard requires, and a reader who disagrees with one of them is disagreeing with this corpus, not with ISO 26262.

Three of the seven guidelines carry the status adopted_with_residual_ambiguity, because the corpus does not hold the evidence to close the question: the ASIL derivation's exposure input (GDL-001), the disagreement between an execution record's classification and its environment prose together with two unexercised enum members (GDL-003), and the absence of a mixed-provenance value for records that are partly observed and partly synthetic (GDL-005). GDL-006 records that the corpus does not yet fully satisfy its own gap rule.

This record cannot be reviewed by the process that wrote it. It was authored by the same automated process that authored the records whose interpretations it fixes, which is the independence absence recorded as RSK-003, and it therefore has no standing as a confirmation of its own guidelines.

No guideline is backed by a human decision, and none is enforceable: nothing in the corpus's validation suite checks that a record follows these guidelines, so they are conventions a reader is expected to apply and not rules a machine enforces. The schema requires each guideline to name its rejected alternative, which is the only enforcement that exists.

The evidence anchors are line numbers in a moving tree. They are correct at commit 737c4e18 and will drift as records are revised; a reader who finds an anchor pointing at the wrong line should treat that as a defect in this record and not as a defect in the record it points at.

known_limitations_verbatim.value: 'baselined' rather than 'approved' or 'reviewed': this record is the output of an automated authoring pass and no human has confirmed it. It is in the same position as the fifteen review records it describes the limits of.

outcome_record._ledger_note: packet_first_commit is the git commit that FIRST contained the archived signed packet. It proves WHEN and IN WHAT STATE the packet was committed. It does NOT prove who read it, and nothing in the corpus makes an approval unforgeable. See docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.md
outcome_record._note: Fields a human or a later process may fill AFTER a signature exists. Empty here; present so the outcome can be captured without editing the generator. Since APPROVAL-LEDGER-A1 the decision is recorded in the append-only ledger at docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl, and these fields cross-reference that entry rather than being the record of it.

questions_for_human.question: As the safety_engineer for this safety record, do you agree that "Corpus interpretation guidelines: the seven interpretation choices this corpus had to make, and the alternative each one refused" is a correct and complete statement of hazard analysis, safety goals, FSR/TSR allocation, safety analyses, the safety case?
questions_for_human.why_this_needs_a_human: Correctness of engineering content is not derivable from the repository. The corpus can prove the record is well-formed and internally consistent; it cannot prove the engineering is right.

questions_for_human.question: This record is labelled origin=`derived`, not observed. Is the derivation reproducible from what it names, or does it assert more than its sources carry?
questions_for_human.why_this_needs_a_human: Derivation is a human act. The corpus can check that the named sources exist; it cannot check that the conclusion follows from them.

questions_for_human.question: No other record in this corpus reviews this one. Is it in fact unreviewed, and does that matter for what you are signing?
questions_for_human.what_in_this_packet_bears_on_it: What is already checked, below: the review coverage column for this record.
questions_for_human.why_this_needs_a_human: Approving an unreviewed record is close to meaningless: the packet gives you the record and the machine checks, not a second reader's reasoning. Say so in the comments if you accept that.

questions_for_human.question: For each standards mapping: is the cited clause the right obligation for this work product, and is the status right?
questions_for_human.why_this_needs_a_human: Clause selection is a reading of a standard, not a property of the repository.

conventions_taken_from_the_vocabulary_re: Safe state, degraded state: read the set from the declaring record - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-002 and VOC-AMB-015
ASIL: read as a classification only where an asil_justification derives it; QM and not_applicable both read as absence - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-003
Fault reaction: read by record type, object on a requirement and list on a concept - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-004
Independence: four readings keyed on the field name - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-005
Freedom from interference: the analysed record and the assumed barrier claim are different questions - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-008
Execution kind: the classification governs and the environment prose does not - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-012
Origin: source_observed, derived and synthetic bound every other field on a record - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 term 'origin'
Artefact identifier: resolve as the pair (profile, id) - FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 VOC-AMB-001
record_verbatim.derivation_method: Each guideline was selected because records in this corpus demonstrably had to choose: the selection test was that two or more records made the same choice in a way that a reader could have made differently, or that a record states the choice in its own words. For each, the corpus's own text for the choice was located and cited, and then the alternative was sought - the reading a competent reader would bring - and the refusal was grounded in a second record or in a governance file, never in the author's preference. Where the corpus could not settle the question, the guideline says so in `not_settled_by_this_guideline` and carries the review status adopted_with_residual_ambiguity: three of the seven do. Counts quoted inside a guideline are counts measured on this tree and are reproducible from the evidence anchor given beside them.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Treating the `asil` field as a determination wherever it appears - the reading a reader brings to a field called ASIL on a safety record.
guidelines.consequences: A reader deciding whether a class is usable must look for the derivation, not the value. Where it is absent, the class is an allocation the reference project made for its own internal consistency and is not evidence about any product. If a future HARA were to classify the current or temperature supervision requirements, those requirements would have to be re-argued rather than re-labelled, because no derivation exists for them today.
guidelines.convention: Read an `asil` value as a classification only where the record carries an `asil_justification` that derives it from named severity and exposure ratings. Derivation is: take the hazardous event from the malfunctioning behaviour, take severity S and exposure E from the operational situation in which it occurs, read the class from the Part 3 severity/exposure determination table, and take the highest class among the hazardous events the safety goal covers. Controllability is recorded but does not enter the determination; it fixes how precisely the operational situation must be described. In this corpus exactly two record identifiers carry such a derivation - FB2-SAF-SGO-000001 in both profiles - and the corpus recomputes the class from the ratings rather than restating it, then compares the result with the value on the record and records that they agree. Where a record carries `asil_allocation_scope` instead, the class was read BACK from the reference project's own chain rather than derived, and the field says so in the words 'reconstructed_back_inference'. Every `asil` value that is neither of those is an allocation reference or an absence marker and is not a classification.

evidence.establishes: The method, stated as the derivation sequence and naming the Part 3 clause references it uses.
`derived_asil_matches_record` is true: the class was recomputed from the ratings and compared with the record.
`classification_status` is 'hypothetical' and `scope_of_this_classification` states in terms that this is not a determination for the real product and that no HARA has been performed for it.

THE UNEVIDENCED INPUT. `exposure.evidence_status` reads 'NOT EVIDENCED. The hazard record states no duty cycle, no mission profile, no fleet statistic and no charge-cycle data. The rating is an authored input.' and continues: 'S3 with E3 is ASIL_C, so the entire classification is one exposure step away from being a class lower, and the input that decides it is the one input in this derivation with no evidence behind it.'
`classification_kind: reconstructed_back_inference` - the vocabulary for a class read back rather than derived, on the as_is hardware requirements.

`open_item` records the consequence for the three system requirements that carry no ASIL: the absence of a recorded derivation is stated to be a property of this corpus, not a demonstrated property of the product.
A security requirement records its reason for carrying no class: ISO 26262 does not allocate an ASIL to a security requirement, so the field is an absence rather than a determination.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: No ASIL in this corpus has an evidenced exposure rating. The one derivation that exists rests on an authored S3, E4 and C3, and the record itself names the exposure as the input that decides the outcome and as unevidenced. Establishing S and E on evidence is work that has not been done, and it is the reason the classification is recorded as hypothetical rather than as a determination.
guidelines.question: This corpus writes an ASIL into an `asil` field. From what is that class derived, and which of its inputs can a reader rely on?
guidelines.title: How an ASIL is obtained here, and the one input that is not evidenced
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because the field carries a class on 35 records and a derivation on two of them. The other 33 carry either a back-inferred allocation or an absence marker, and a reader who cannot tell them apart will read an ASIL D on a network-security requirement as a classification. The corpus has already found this class of error once: an earlier audit flagged the unqualified ASIL on as_is records, and the corpus's response was not to delete the values - which would have left the fictional project's allocation silently unallocated - but to add the `asil_allocation_scope` field that declares them reconstructed and states that the real product has never had a hazard analysis and risk assessment.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Marking the records `approved` once the automated review suite passes, or treating the fifteen reviews as confirmation measures.
guidelines.consequences: No reader of this corpus may treat anything in it as approved, authorised, or credited as product verification. A release recommendation that reads 'conditional release for development use only' means exactly that and nothing more, and the safety case skeleton carries it with `production_authorized` false. The fifteen reviews may be read as evidence that an automated pass ran and what it found - including the findings that remain open - and as nothing else. To move any record out of pending, a person who did not author the corpus has to do it, and nothing in this corpus can substitute for that.
guidelines.convention: `human_approval_status: pending` asserts that no person has reviewed, confirmed or approved the record, and nothing else. It is the whole of the field's meaning: it is not a criticism, not a provisional pass and not a statement that the record is waiting on something. Alongside it, `production_authorized` is false and `product_verification_credit` is false on every record, and the role-and-review policy sets both by policy rather than by assessment. An automated review does NOT change any of the three, and it is never an independence: the fifteen review records in this corpus were all produced by the same process that produced the records they review, and the corpus's own risk register records the absence of an independent confirmation reviewer as a risk whose effect is that the safety case cannot be assembled at all.

evidence.establishes: The field's four admitted values: pending, approved, rejected, not_required. A reader can see that only four readings are available and that 'not_required' would be a positive claim, not the default.
The policy's approval vocabulary, its `synthetic_decision_label` requiring fictional role identities to be stated as such, and `production_authorized: false` set by policy.
The review-policy rule: AI reviews are automated reviews; distinct agent sessions are not organizational independence or human confirmation measures; real human approval remains pending.
`safety_critical_additional: separated_challenge_pass` - the safety-critical review obligation the corpus names, satisfied by two challenge reviews that are themselves automated.

`reviewer_identity` names the role, a session, the model and the note 'AI-assisted review; human confirmation pending', so the review record's own identity field records who reviewed and that a human did not.

RSK-003: the condition is that every review in the corpus is an automated AI review in a coding-agent session; the consequence is stated as 'The safety case cannot be assembled at all'; the mitigation that was performed is to record the absence on every review record, and the escalation that was not performed is engaging an independent reviewer.
SUP.1's own statement: the quality engineer may not review an artifact it authored, and in this corpus that independence 'is stated and not achieved'.
The confirmation measure, recorded as a constraint on the record: 'Independent confirmation for ASIL D (not achieved in synthetic)'.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: The corpus has no record of an attempted human review, so this guideline cannot say what a human reviewer would have found. It can only say that none was asked.
guidelines.question: Every record in this corpus carries `human_approval_status: pending`. What does that field assert, what does it withhold, and does an automated review change it?
guidelines.title: What `human_approval_status: pending` means here, and why no automated review is an independence
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because the corpus's own policy says in terms that AI reviews are automated reviews, that distinct agent sessions are not organisational independence and not human confirmation measures, and that real human approval remains pending. The rule is not a caution: the validator rejects `human_approval_status: approved` as a high-severity finding on any record and rejects `production_authorized: true` as critical, so a corpus that passed its reviews and promoted them would fail its own suite. The supporting-process record for SUP.1 states the position without hedging: the independence of the quality engineer 'is stated and not achieved', because every review in the corpus is an automated review produced by the same process that produced the artifacts and no human reviewer exists. And the safety plan records the confirmation measure as 'Independent confirmation for ASIL D (not achieved in synthetic)'.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Reading a record's `environment.hardware` prose at face value - so a record whose execution_kind is synthetic_fixture and whose environment reads 'x86_64 Linux host (simulated)' would be counted as a host run.
guidelines.consequences: The corpus's own measured position is that there are zero target-hardware runs. Two enum members are never used by any record, so the vocabulary is declared wider than the corpus exercises and a reader must not infer from the enum that a simulation run happened. A blocked outcome is a result, not a gap in the record: it is the honest outcome for the 23 records whose execution_kind is none, and reporting them as 'not run' would understate what was established about why they could not run.
guidelines.convention: Read `execution_kind` as the classification and `environment` as prose; where the two disagree about the KIND of platform, `execution_kind` governs. The four members are not interchangeable and are not all evidence: `synthetic_fixture` means the expectation was met by a fixture, so a `pass` confirms the fixture and not the product; `actual_host_run` means real product code executed on a developer machine, so a pass is evidence about the code and not about the hardware it runs on; `actual_simulation_run` means an executed model with captured logs, which the corpus policy requires to have both; `actual_target_hardware_run` is the only member that constitutes product-hardware evidence and no record in this corpus carries it. `execution_kind` is orthogonal to `outcome`: a blocked outcome is the correct outcome for a run that could not happen, and planning is not execution however complete the plan.

evidence.establishes: The `execution_kind` enum of five members, with the description naming actual_target_hardware_run as the only member that constitutes product-hardware evidence.
The `outcome` enum of five members, described as orthogonal in intent: pass, fail, inconclusive, not_run, blocked.
The policy description: 'Orthogonal to outcome. Planning is not execution. Fabricated simulation-looking numbers are synthetic_fixture.'
The rule an actual_simulation_run must satisfy: it requires an executed model and captured logs.
The rule that produces blocked rather than success: missing target hardware or proprietary compilers.
The rule that keeps self-checks from counting as product evidence: generated consistency-check results validate the corpus, not the BMS product.
`execution_kind: synthetic_fixture` on a record whose outcome is pass and whose title names a synthetic fixture.
The same record's `environment.hardware` reads 'x86_64 Linux host (simulated)' - prose describing a host, classification saying fixture. This is the disagreement the convention exists for.
The tool's own split: HOST_EXECUTION_KINDS are the host and simulation members and are treated as developer infrastructure, NOT product-hardware evidence.
DECLARED_EXECUTION_KINDS: every member the schema admits, which is five, against three the corpus actually uses.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: The disagreement between a record's classification and its environment prose is preserved rather than corrected, because rewriting an execution record is a content revision this authoring pass does not own. Two of the five enum members are unexercised, so this guideline cannot say what evidence a simulation run in THIS corpus would have carried - only what the schema requires of one.
guidelines.question: The `execution_kind` field distinguishes a fixture, a host run, a simulation run and a run on the product's own hardware. Which member applies to a record, what does that member license a reader to conclude, and where does the record's own prose disagree with it?
guidelines.title: How the four run classes are told apart, and what each one implies as evidence
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because that record exists and would be miscounted. The field is a free string and it is written by the same process that writes the classification, and on at least one record the two describe different kinds of platform. The enum exists precisely so that the classification is machine-checkable and the prose is not, and the coverage dimension that counts target-hardware evidence reads `execution_kind` alone for exactly this reason. The policy is explicit in the same direction twice: missing target hardware or proprietary compilers is blocked and not a fabricated success, and generated consistency-check results validate the corpus and not the BMS product.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Allowing `related_to` as a general-purpose 'these two are connected' link, which is what its name invites.
guidelines.consequences: A reader checking whether a requirement is reached must be able to state the chain as a sequence of named dependencies. A chain assembled from `related_to` states nothing about what was done at each step, and the corpus's own trace tool refuses to walk one. Conversely a reader who finds a chain that dead-ends should read that as a real gap rather than as a missing link, because the corpus would have refused to add one that did not mean anything.
guidelines.convention: A link carries engineering meaning when its relation type states what the target IS for the source, its endpoints resolve in the same profile, and it carries the required metadata - rationale, provenance, review_state and change_suspect_status. The seventeen accepted relation types each name a directed dependency: a requirement refines or is allocated_to, a design implements, a test measure verifies or validates, an execution is result_of, evidence supports a claim, a safety mechanism mitigates, an interface is specified_by, an element consumes or produces, an artifact depends_on or is constrained_by, an artifact is reviewed_by, a request changes an artifact, a new revision supersedes an old one. `related_to` is NOT one of them: it is admitted by the type validator so that a mutation can introduce it, and it is rejected as forbidden wherever it appears in a canonical registry, because a relation that asserts no kind of dependence satisfies no coverage obligation and would let a chain be closed over a gap that has been declared but not engineered. It is also excluded from the trace-chain traversal for the same reason.

evidence.establishes: STRICT_FORBIDDEN_RELATION_TYPES is exactly {related_to} - one relation held out, by name.
`link_metadata_required` names the four metadata fields a link must carry, which is what makes a link auditable rather than merely present.
`change_suspect_status` on the same list: a link records whether it has been re-examined, so a stale link says so rather than looking current.

`claims[].arguments[].evidence` - the strongest form in this corpus: the claim names its arguments and each argument names the records it rests on, which is `supports` applied to evidence rather than a general association.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: The corpus does not classify links as 'legitimate' versus 'bookkeeping' by any recorded test beyond the type set and the metadata requirement. A link of an accepted type whose rationale is uninformative would pass; this guideline states the intent but the corpus has no mechanism that measures it.
guidelines.question: The corpus carries 547 typed links. What makes a link carry engineering meaning, and why is one relation type held out of the canonical registries entirely?
guidelines.title: What counts as a trace link, and why `related_to` is forbidden
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because it is the one relation that says nothing about the direction or the kind of dependence, so a link registry full of them would look connected while asserting nothing. The corpus's own code states the consequence: the relation is excluded from the trace chain because following it 'would let the chain pass over a gap that has been declared but not engineered'. That is the same failure the corpus exists to prevent - a trace that appears to reach a requirement without anything having been derived, allocated or verified on the way. The decision is also self-consistent in the strict direction: a bookkeeping link would be refused, so a reader who finds a chain that does not reach is being told something true.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Treating `derived` as 'source_observed but with more words', so that a derived record inherits the evidentiary weight of an observed one.
guidelines.consequences: A reader must read `origin` before reading anything else on a record, because it bounds every other field. A `derived` record's numbers are reproducible from the pinned source but its judgements are not; a `synthetic` record's numbers are not about the product at all. Where a record mixes the two - and several do, the hardware configuration baseline being one - the record is expected to say which parts are which in its own prose, and a reader who skips that prose will misattribute a datasheet figure to the product.
guidelines.convention: Read `origin: source_observed` as 'this content was read from the pinned source and can be re-read at commit 308028fb'; read `origin: derived` as 'this content is a reasoned or mechanical transformation of the pinned source, reproducible but not observed'; read `origin: synthetic` as 'this content describes the fictional reference project and asserts nothing about the product'. The three are not a quality ranking and one does not imply another: a `derived` record may be a reconstruction read BACK from the corpus's own reference project, in which case the record says so with `classification_kind: reconstructed_back_inference` and declares that it is not a determination for the product. The rule is enforced in one direction by the validator and not the other: an `as_is` record carrying `origin: synthetic` is a high-severity profile-contamination finding, but a `synthetic_reference` record carrying `source_observed` is not an error, because a record may legitimately be derived from real observations while describing a fictional project. Never read a synthetic-origin field as evidence about the product; the corpus's own import contract says so in terms.

evidence.establishes: The enum: source_observed, derived, synthetic, with the description 'Provenance origin category'.
The validator: an as_is artefact with origin=synthetic is a high-severity profile-contamination finding. One direction is enforced; the other is not, and that asymmetry is deliberate.

A revision-history entry recording the change: the asil_allocation_scope field was added and the origin moved from source_observed to derived, because an audit flagged the record as asserting an unqualified ASIL on an as_is profile record.
The provenance_note behind that change on the same record: 'Part observed, part modelled, so labelled derived'.

The import contract: the as_is profile admits origin in {source_observed, derived}, the synthetic_reference profile may add synthetic, and importing systems MUST NOT treat synthetic origin as observed evidence.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: The corpus has no rule for a record that is partly observed and partly synthetic with no prose separating the two, and it has no `origin` value meaning 'mixed'. Such a record can only be handled by reading it.
guidelines.question: The `origin` field admits three values. Which one applies to a given piece of content, and what may a reader conclude from it?
guidelines.title: When a record is `derived`, when it is `synthetic`, and when it is `source_observed`
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because derivation is exactly where this corpus's own worst errors were. The as_is hardware and software requirements were changed from `source_observed` to `derived` precisely because their ASIL allocations were reconstructions read back from the reference project and not observations of the product; the revision history records that an audit flagged them and that the field added in response declares the reconstruction. Reading a derived record as observed would reinstate the exact defect that revision removed, and would do so silently, because both values sit in the same field.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Authoring a thin record of the missing family - a placeholder safety plan, a stub hardware detailed design, a requirements file with a handful of entries - so that the family reads as populated.
guidelines.consequences: A family with no record must read as a family with no record. The three forms above all exist so that the absence is visible in a place a reader looks, and all three carry the same three things: what was searched for, why the search found nothing, and what would close it. A reader who finds a declared gap can act on it; a reader who finds a thin record cannot, and worse, the thin record will be counted.
guidelines.convention: A gap is recorded as an ABSENCE WITH A SEARCH, not as a record and not as a placeholder. The three forms in use are: (1) a Markdown note in an otherwise empty directory, stating what was searched for, what was found, why no record was created, which coverage-plan entries the absence affects, and what would legitimately close it - deliberately not a JSON record, because a declaration of emptiness is not an artefact and forcing it into the artefact model would need an invented id and an artefact_type outside the registry; (2) a record whose artefact_type names the gap, so the absence is indexed and countable rather than silent; (3) an explicit ABSENT or open_item entry inside a record that does exist, stating which expected family is missing and what the consequence is. In all three forms the corpus records the consequence for the coverage plan rather than leaving the gap to be inferred from silence. The rule against closing a gap by inventing content is the corpus's own and it is stated in the same notes: only real work closes a gap, not a new file.

evidence.establishes: The gap-as-record form: FB2-HW-HDD-000001 exists, is indexed, and its artefact_type names hardware_detailed_design_gap rather than borrowing a real one.
The register form: ten open deficiencies are recorded as a register rather than left as unmeasured absence.
The note form: the file declares itself not an artefact, states that it has no id, is not a link endpoint, and is deliberately not JSON.
The search that establishes the absence: the searches actually run against the pinned tree, with their results, so the claim 'nothing was found' is checkable.

The rule against inventing a record, stated as a consequence: writing the record would have 'created a new overclaim in exchange for closing one, which is the exact failure mode this corpus exists to prevent'.

What would legitimately close the gap: only real work - an actual elicited and baselined requirements specification, or a policy permitting derived reconstruction in the as_is profile, neither of which exists.
The correction in the other direction, recorded on the plan itself: a disposition reading `mapped` was demoted because the record it named carries none of the three things the disposition claimed.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: Two coverage-plan entries still read higher than their evidence in this corpus's own assessment of itself - the note above names four of them and this authoring pass does not own the plan's other entries - so this guideline states the rule and the corpus does not yet fully satisfy it. Nothing here closes that.
guidelines.question: Several families of record do not exist in this corpus. How does the corpus say so, and what is the rule against filling the hole?
guidelines.title: How a declared gap is recorded, and when a gap must not be closed by inventing content
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because a thin record is indistinguishable from a real one by every measure the corpus reports. The population coverage dimension counts records by family, the traceability gates count links, and a stub with no content and no links moves none of them except the family count - which is the only thing that would improve. The corpus met this exact temptation and refused it: the coverage plan records that MAN.3, MAN.5, MAN.6 and PIM.3 read `mapped` when no project plan, risk register, measurement plan or improvement record existed, and the note that documents the search says in terms that only real work closes the gap and that these four were reported rather than fixed so the task's change set stayed inside its scope. One of the corrections made by that pass went the other way, from `mapped` to `gap`, precisely because a family had no record.

guidelines.alternative_rejected: Fixing the product defect once the corpus has found it - and the corpus is in a position to do so, because it can read and write the source tree.
guidelines.consequences: A defect found in the product is a finding to be reported, not a task to be completed inside the corpus. The corpus may analyse it, re-examine it, withdraw an earlier reading of it, and record the consequence for coverage - and it may do none of the things that would make the observation unrepeatable. The consequence for a reader is that a defect reported here is still a defect in the product, and the product has not been improved by the corpus having found it.
guidelines.convention: A defect found in the product is RECORDED and the product is left untouched. Three record forms carry product observations and all three are observations: a `deviation` record, which requires the affected file, the affected symbol, the affected lines and an evidence quote from the pinned source and is as_is-only by construction because it reports an in-source suppression annotation; a `test_measure` or `execution` record carrying a real failure with the numbers as they were; and a review finding, which is raised and then dispositioned. When the corpus's own earlier reading turned out to be wrong, the response was to withdraw the claim in the record's own revision history rather than to leave it standing, and it withdrew a substantial one - an earlier round's attribution of thirty build failures to real defects in foxBMS source was corrected and most of it withdrawn. The rule that makes this safe is stated on the execution records themselves and repeated at every revision: no product source was touched and no result was adjusted to make a test pass.

evidence.establishes: The deviation form: an as_is record whose id is FB2-SW-DEV-000012 and whose subject is an integer-to-pointer cast in a DMA buffer address in the pinned source.
`deviation_type` classifies what kind of departure it is, so the observation is a classification of the source and not a verdict on the product.

`reanalysis_justification` re-examines an earlier justification on re-reading the source and finds it was asserted rather than evidenced - a self-correction of the corpus's own reading of the product.
The withdrawal: 'THE PREVIOUS ATTRIBUTION OF THE BUILD FAILURES IS CORRECTED AND MOST OF IT WITHDRAWN. The prior round reported 30 real defects in foxBMS source...'

The rule, restated at five revisions of the same record: 'No product source was touched and no result was adjusted to make a test pass. This record is a HOST run and carries no production verification credit.'

A product observation about the test suite itself: five test files recorded green whose single test-case function calls the function under test and asserts nothing. Recorded as vacuous, and the tests left as they are.
`no_universal_review_from_sample: true` - the reason a sample of records cannot stand for the whole, and the reason every recorded observation names what it actually covered.

guidelines.not_settled_by_this_guideline: The corpus cannot raise a defect against the product in any process that would route it to the people who maintain it; there is no such channel in this corpus. The records are the whole of the reporting.
guidelines.question: Several records in this corpus are observations of the pinned product that a reader would call defects. What happened to the product, and what is the rule?
guidelines.title: A defect the corpus found in the product is recorded, not fixed in the product
guidelines.why_the_alternative_was_refused: Because a fix would destroy the only thing the observation is evidence of, and would make the corpus the author of the product it claims to observe. The as_is profile may record only what the pinned source demonstrates, and its authority over the implementation is read-only; a corpus that edited the product could no longer cite a commit it had itself moved. The corpus has also been caught out on the other side - attributing thirty build failures to real defects in product source and then having to withdraw most of the attribution - which is the reason the rule is stated in terms of what the record may claim rather than in terms of what the reviewer is confident of. Reporting a real failure as a pass would make the corpus's coverage figures meaningless, and the ten red host tests are reported as red for exactly that reason.

record_verbatim.lifecycle_status_note: 'baselined' rather than 'approved' or 'reviewed': this record is the output of an automated authoring pass and no human has confirmed it. It is in the same position as the fifteen review records it describes the limits of.
limitations: These are the interpretations this corpus made. They are not the interpretations the standard requires, and a reader who disagrees with one of them is disagreeing with this corpus, not with ISO 26262.

Three of the seven guidelines carry the status adopted_with_residual_ambiguity, because the corpus does not hold the evidence to close the question: the ASIL derivation's exposure input (GDL-001), the disagreement between an execution record's classification and its environment prose together with two unexercised enum members (GDL-003), and the absence of a mixed-provenance value for records that are partly observed and partly synthetic (GDL-005). GDL-006 records that the corpus does not yet fully satisfy its own gap rule.

This record cannot be reviewed by the process that wrote it. It was authored by the same automated process that authored the records whose interpretations it fixes, which is the independence absence recorded as RSK-003, and it therefore has no standing as a confirmation of its own guidelines.

No guideline is backed by a human decision, and none is enforceable: nothing in the corpus's validation suite checks that a record follows these guidelines, so they are conventions a reader is expected to apply and not rules a machine enforces. The schema requires each guideline to name its rejected alternative, which is the only enforcement that exists.

The evidence anchors are line numbers in a moving tree. They are correct at commit 737c4e18 and will drift as records are revised; a reader who finds an anchor pointing at the wrong line should treat that as a defect in this record and not as a defect in the record it points at.
record_verbatim.purpose: This corpus had to make interpretation choices that a reader cannot recover from the records alone: how far an ASIL field may be read, what a pending approval withholds, which of four run classes a record belongs to, which of seventeen link relations say something, which of three provenance values applies, how to say that something is missing, and what to do about a defect found in the product. Each choice had an obvious alternative and the alternative was refused for a reason that rests on a record in this corpus rather than on preference. The purpose of this record is to make the refusals arguable: a reader who disagrees can name the guideline, read the alternative, and decide which of the two is right. A record that only stated what the corpus does would not be worth writing, because the reader could obtain that from the records themselves.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Treating the `asil` field as a determination wherever it appears - the reading a reader brings to a field called ASIL on a safety record.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because the field carries a class on 35 records and a derivation on two of them.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Marking the records `approved` once the automated review suite passes, or treating the fifteen reviews as confirmation measures.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because the corpus's own policy says in terms that AI reviews are automated reviews, that distinct agent sessions are not organisational independence and not human confirmation measures, and that real human approval remains pending.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Reading a record's `environment.hardware` prose at face value - so a record whose execution_kind is synthetic_fixture and whose environment reads 'x86_64 Linux host (simulated)' would be counted as a host run.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because that record exists and would be miscounted.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Allowing `related_to` as a general-purpose 'these two are connected' link, which is what its name invites.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because it is the one relation that says nothing about the direction or the kind of dependence, so a link registry full of them would look connected while asserting nothing.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Treating `derived` as 'source_observed but with more words', so that a derived record inherits the evidentiary weight of an observed one.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because derivation is exactly where this corpus's own worst errors were.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Authoring a thin record of the missing family - a placeholder safety plan, a stub hardware detailed design, a requirements file with a handful of entries - so that the family reads as populated.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because a thin record is indistinguishable from a real one by every measure the corpus reports.

refusals_summary.alternative_refused: Fixing the product defect once the corpus has found it - and the corpus is in a position to do so, because it can read and write the source tree.
refusals_summary.one_line_reason: Because a fix would destroy the only thing the observation is evidence of, and would make the corpus the author of the product it claims to observe.

revision_history.author: safety_engineer
revision_history.description: First issue. Authored because the coverage plan's ISO 26262 Part 10 entry had no backing artefact. Seven guidelines, each naming the obvious alternative it refuses and the corpus evidence for refusing it: how an ASIL is obtained here and which of its inputs is unevidenced; what human_approval_status pending means and why an automated review is not an independence; how a fixture, a host run, a simulation run and a target-hardware run are told apart and what each implies; what makes a trace link carry meaning and why one relation type is forbidden in a canonical registry; when a record is derived, synthetic or source_observed; how a declared gap is recorded and why a gap must not be closed by inventing a record; and what happens to a defect the corpus finds in the product, which is that the corpus records it and does not fix it. Term conventions are referenced from FB2-SAF-VOC-000001 rather than restated. human_approval_status remains pending, production_authorized remains false and product_verification_credit remains false.

record_verbatim.rights_statement: No normative text of ISO 26262 or of any other standard is reproduced, paraphrased, translated or summarised here. Clause references appear as identifiers in the form the existing records already use - for example 'Part 3, Clause 6', 'Part 6, Clause 9', 'Part 10, Clause 4' - and nothing more. Every guideline rests on this corpus's own records, its own governance files and its own tool, and each cites the file and line it rests on so a reader can check the argument rather than accept it. The rights position of the corpus is in docs/artifacts/governance/standards-lock.json and is not widened or narrowed here.

standards_mappings.rationale: Guidelines on how the standard is to be understood and applied. This record supplies the interpretation decisions THIS CORPUS made, which is the only form in which a Part 10 reference can be honestly discharged: it records the corpus's own choices and their grounds, and no clause text is reproduced or paraphrased.

The interpretations concerning the analysis of the technical concepts. The safety concepts are records in this corpus and their open questions are recorded in the records themselves, in the fields named open_limits, open_item and not_settled_by_this_guideline. This entry is partially_mapped because this record covers the interpretation rules and not the analysis content, which lives in the concepts.

record_verbatim.title: Corpus interpretation guidelines: the seven interpretation choices this corpus had to make, and the alternative each one refused
what_this_record_does_not_assert: It does not state how ISO 26262 is to be interpreted. It states how this corpus interpreted the questions, and each guideline is defensible only against this corpus's own evidence.
It does not make any record compliant with anything. A guideline followed by every record would still leave this corpus unapproved, unauthorised, and without a target-hardware run.

It does not assert human approval, production authorisation, product verification credit, ISO 26262 conformity, certification, tool qualification or an ASPICE capability level. human_approval_status is pending, production_authorized is false and product_verification_credit is false.
It does not close any gap. GDL-006 says how gaps are recorded; it does not record a new one and it does not close an existing one.
It does not repair the product. GDL-007 says the corpus leaves product defects in place, and this record does so too.

shape_note: Deliberately not shaped like a corpus record: no top-level id, profile, artifact_type or source_refs, so that generating packets cannot change any coverage number. See the module docstring of make_review_packets.py.

_contract.digest_note: The digests below are already filled in. Copy them; do not type them. Run `make_review_packets.py --transcribe FB2-SAF-GDL-000001` to have them printed as a pasteable block.
_contract.grant_is: any value other than "pending" or absent
required_elements: 2. approved_by - a named individual, not a role and not a team

3. role - a role_id declared in role-and-review-policy.json#/roles - plus independence{owner_role, satisfied, evidence, policy_ref}; the approving role must differ from owner_role AND from the author of the last content revision
4. date - ISO-8601, checked by grammar and by parse

5. review_packet{path, sha256, record_sha256_at_signing}; path must resolve to a packet.json on disk under docs/artifacts/reviews/signed ONLY - the regenerated tree docs/artifacts/reviews/packets is NOT admissible, because it is rewritten on every regeneration and would destroy your evidence; sha256 must equal that file's bytes now; record_sha256_at_signing must equal this packet's integrity.record_sha256; target.record_id and target.profile must both name this record

6. approval_ledger_ref{ledger_id, entry_sha256} naming your entry in docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl. It is approval METADATA, not content: it is excluded from the record's content digest and is never a revision_history entry, so recording it neither bumps the revision nor stales a link. NEVER record the approval in revision_history - doing so stales every link pinning this revision and invalidates every stored review digest. See docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.md

signature_block._packet_sha256_note: The digest of this packet.json's own bytes. It is deliberately left null rather than filled, because a file cannot contain its own digest. Compute it with `shasum -a 256`, or use `--transcribe`, which resolves it.
signature_block._recording: Archive the signed packet under docs/artifacts/reviews/signed/<profile>/<id>.json, then record the approval as human_approval_status plus an approval_evidence.human_approval block on the record, plus approval_ledger_ref naming one appended line in docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl. Do NOT add a revision_history entry: see docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.md.
signature_block._rule: Empty by construction. No automated process may fill this. Filling it in is the only thing that changes human_approval_status on the record. As of 2026-10-04 (amendment APPROVAL-RULE-A1) the corpus rule human_approval_rejected is an EVIDENCE requirement, not a prohibition: a properly evidenced approval is ACCEPTED and keeps `corpus.py check` green, while a bare grant value is still rejected. What the validator reads is contract.approval_evidence_block below; it fails if any of its six elements is missing, and the finding names which.

signature_policy: The signature block below is empty by construction. This tool has no code path that writes a decision, an approval, a signature or an execution verdict. Filling it is a human action. As of 2026-10-04 (amendment APPROVAL-RULE-A1) the corpus ACCEPTS a properly evidenced approval rather than banning the value outright, so this rule now has to carry the evidence contract in full: see signature_block._contract. Since the same day (amendment APPROVAL-LEDGER-A1) the approval is recorded in the append-only ledger at docs/artifacts/governance/approval-ledger.jsonl and the record keeps only a reference to it, so recording your signature neither bumps the revision nor invalidates any review digest.

target.primary_key_rule: ID-RULE-004-A1: an artefact identifier is unique within its profile; two records of different profiles may carry the same identifier string.
